intro: Warm-season grasses (bermudagrass, zoysiagrass, St. Augustinegrass and centipedegrass) grow in the heat and go tan and dormant after frost. Almost all the work happens while the lawn is green: prevent crabgrass before it sprouts, feed from full green-up to late summer, mow often, and stop nitrogen well before the first frost.

principles.title: Feed only while it's green
principles.text: The feeding year runs from full spring green-up to about 6–8 weeks before the first frost. Fertilizer on dormant or half-green turf feeds weeds, and late nitrogen invites winter injury and large patch.

principles.title: Match nitrogen to the grass
principles.text: Bermudagrass and St. Augustinegrass use 2–4 lb N per 1,000 sq ft a year. Zoysiagrass needs 1–2 lb. Centipedegrass needs only ½–1 lb, and more than that is the usual cause of centipede decline.

principles.title: Mow at the right height, often
principles.text: Bermudagrass 1–2 in, zoysiagrass 1–2.5 in, centipedegrass 1.5–2 in, St. Augustinegrass 2.5–4 in. Mowing too high builds thatch in bermuda and zoysia; mowing St. Augustine too low thins it and lets weeds in.

principles.title: Water deeply, not daily
principles.text: Water when the lawn shows stress (blue-gray color, folded leaves, footprints that stay), then apply about 1 in. Bermudagrass and zoysiagrass ride out drought by going dormant; St. Augustinegrass and centipedegrass need a soak every 2–3 weeks to survive one.

principles.title: Stop weeds before they sprout
principles.text: A spring pre-emergent stops crabgrass and a fall one stops annual bluegrass and winter weeds. For anything sprayed on the leaves, check the label for your grass: St. Augustinegrass and centipedegrass are injured by products that are safe on bermudagrass.

principles.title: Repair in early summer
principles.text: Sod, plug, seed, aerate and dethatch from late spring to midsummer, when the grass is growing fastest and has months to recover before dormancy.

nNote: All nitrogen goes on between full green-up and late summer. The bars show this plan's feedings for your grass, moved to your local calendar.
mowNote: Mow whenever the grass is growing, at the height for your grass. Raise it half an inch in shade, in drought, and for the last few cuts before dormancy.

keyDates.why: Crabgrass sprouts once the soil warms. A pre-emergent only works if it is down first.

keyDates.what: First feeding: 1 lb N per 1,000 sq ft (½ lb for centipedegrass)
keyDates.why: Roots take up nitrogen only once the grass is actively growing.

keyDates.what: Sod, plug or seed bare areas; aerate and dethatch if needed
keyDates.why: Warm soil and a long season ahead give the fastest establishment and recovery.

keyDates.what: Second feeding for bermudagrass, zoysiagrass and St. Augustinegrass
keyDates.why: Keeps the lawn dense enough to crowd out summer weeds.

keyDates.what: Last nitrogen for bermudagrass and St. Augustinegrass
keyDates.why: Later nitrogen delays dormancy and raises the risk of winter injury.

keyDates.what: Fall pre-emergent for annual bluegrass and winter weeds
keyDates.why: Winter weeds sprout in fall and take over the dormant lawn if nothing stops them.

keyDates.what: Watch for large patch; preventive fungicide only for lawns hit every year
keyDates.why: The fungus is active as soil cools; treating after patches show does little.

water.short: Wait for the lawn to ask: a blue-gray color, folded leaves or footprints that stay. Then put down about **1 in** early in the morning. In most of the Southeast, rain covers much of what the lawn needs; in dry climates, plan on watering every week in summer.
tunaCan: Set out 4–6 straight-sided cans across the area your sprinkler covers.
Measure the water depth in each can and average them.
Double it for your sprinkler's rate in inches per hour, and save that in the Tools page.

facts.text: Warm-season lawns use roughly 1 in of water a week in summer heat, less in spring and fall, and almost none when dormant.
Light daily watering keeps the surface wet, which grows shallow roots and favors disease. One or two deep soakings a week are better.
Bermudagrass and zoysiagrass survive long droughts by going dormant and green up within a couple of weeks of rain.
St. Augustinegrass and centipedegrass have shallow, above-ground runners and can die in a long drought without an occasional soak.
On clay or slopes, split the watering into two runs 30 minutes apart so it soaks in instead of running off.

blend.title: Sod, plugs or seed?
blend.text: How you establish a warm-season lawn depends on the grass. Plant from late spring to midsummer, when soil is 65°F or warmer.
points: **Bermudagrass:** seed (common types) or sod (hybrid types). Fastest to fill in.
**Zoysiagrass:** sod or plugs; a few varieties come as seed. Slow to spread, so plugs take two seasons.
**St. Augustinegrass:** sod or plugs only. There is no seed.
**Centipedegrass:** seed, sod or plugs. Seed is slow: allow a full season.

seed.cultivarsIntro: Each grass has a place. Pick by your sun, traffic and how much work you want.

cultivars.name: Bermudagrass
cultivars.why: Full sun only. Tough, fast to recover, drought-hardy. Needs the most mowing and feeding, and creeps into beds.

cultivars.name: Zoysiagrass
cultivars.why: Sun to light shade. Dense, soft, low on fertilizer. Slow to establish and slow to recover from damage.

cultivars.name: St. Augustinegrass
cultivars.why: The best warm-season grass for shade. Coarse and lush. Tender in cold winters; watch for chinch bugs.

cultivars.name: Centipedegrass
cultivars.why: The low-maintenance choice for acid, sandy soil. Light green by nature. Dislikes heavy feeding, traffic and high pH.

avoid: Seeding or sodding in fall: the grass goes dormant before it roots.
Fertilizing a new lawn heavily. A starter fertilizer at planting is enough until it is mowed.
Mixing grass types. They differ in color, texture and care, and the mix looks patchy.
Putting down pre-emergent where you plan to seed within 2–4 months.

mowTips: Follow the ⅓ rule: never remove more than a third of the blade in one mowing.
In peak summer growth, that means mowing bermudagrass every 4–7 days.
Leave the clippings. They return nitrogen and do not cause thatch.
Sharpen the blade at least twice a season; a dull blade leaves a gray, frayed lawn.
Mow when the grass is dry, and change direction each time.
A reel mower gives the best cut on bermudagrass and zoysiagrass kept below 1.5 in.
Raise the height half an inch in shade and during drought.
Stop mowing when the lawn goes dormant; do not scalp it in fall.

howTo: Take 10–15 cores or trowel slices, 3–4 in deep, from across the lawn.
Mix them in a clean plastic bucket and remove grass and roots.
Let the soil air-dry, then fill the lab's sample bag or box.
Send it to your state Extension soil lab or drop it at your county Extension office.
Retest every 3 years, or before a renovation.

notes.title: pH matters most for centipedegrass
notes.text: Centipedegrass wants acid soil, pH 5.0–6.0. Lime it only if a test calls for it. Bermudagrass, zoysiagrass and St. Augustinegrass are happy at 6.0–7.0.

notes.title: Phosphorus
notes.text: Many established lawns need none, and several states restrict it. Apply phosphorus only when a soil test shows a shortage or when planting.

notes.title: Potassium
notes.text: Potassium helps with drought and winter hardiness. If your test shows it low, apply it with the last feeding of the year.

notes.title: Compaction
notes.text: Clay and high-traffic lawns benefit from core aeration in early summer. Sandy soil rarely needs it.

more.title: Shade
more.text: Bermudagrass thins quickly with less than 6–8 hours of sun. St. Augustinegrass and some zoysiagrass varieties handle light shade. Under dense trees, mulch or a groundcover does better than any grass.

more.title: Thatch
more.text: A spongy layer more than ½ in thick blocks water and roots. It comes from heavy nitrogen and mowing too high, not from clippings. Dethatch in early summer.

more.title: Winter color
more.text: Dormant tan is normal and healthy. Overseeding bermudagrass with ryegrass gives winter green but slows spring green-up; do not overseed the other warm-season grasses.

more.title: Leaves
more.text: Mulch-mow light leaf cover into the lawn. Rake or bag heavy layers so they do not smother the grass going into dormancy.

more.title: Spring dead spot
more.text: Round dead patches in bermudagrass at green-up are spring dead spot, a root disease that infects in fall. Avoid late nitrogen, relieve compaction, and let the grass creep back in.

more.title: Edges and beds
more.text: Bermudagrass and zoysiagrass invade flower beds by runners. A spade-cut edge or buried edging 6 in deep slows them down.
